claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native thin iron oxide/hydroxide layer before testing.
The native oxide/hydroxide layer is initially self-healing.
The native oxide/hydroxide layer provides temporary corrosion protection at ambient temperature.
The native oxide/hydroxide layer becomes unstable in high-temperature molten-salt environments.
High-temperature thermal cycling induces differential thermal expansion in the oxide/steel system.
High-temperature exposure promotes grain-boundary oxidation in Q235 steel.
Differential expansion and grain-boundary oxidation cause oxide-scale spallation and pore formation.
Scale spallation and pores permit aggressive species to reach the underlying metal and accelerate corrosion.
Slow room-temperature oxidation kinetics foster a coherent passive film on Q235 steel.
Rapid oxidation under cyclic high-temperature salt exposure contributes to protective-scale failure.
Q235 steel will exhibit a lower corrosion rate during room-temperature testing than during cyclic high-temperature molten-salt testing.
Cyclic exposure at approximately 900 °C will produce significant weight gain in Q235 steel.
Cyclic exposure at approximately 900 °C will produce visible oxide-scale spallation.
Cyclic high-temperature molten-salt exposure will degrade the microstructural integrity of Q235 steel.
Alloying or coating with chromium or aluminum can promote a more stable protective oxide scale than that on untreated Q235 steel.
Room-temperature exposure in 3.5 wt% H2SO4 and cyclic exposure at approximately 900 °C in Na2SO4/NaCl/V2O5 are proposed as the two test regimes.
SEM/EDS, XRD, microscopy, mass-change measurements, and room-temperature electrochemical measurements are proposed to assess scale structure and corrosion behavior.
